name: Vestal
lede: Vestal is a dusty grey-mauve from a 1930 American color dictionary, and its name points to the Roman priestesses of Vesta, who were dressed in white.

sections.title: The name and the color
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary lists Vestal as a fashion-and-textile name, first recorded in 1916 [1]. The books we hold give no definition of the color itself, so what the name was meant to suggest is undocumented [1]. The obvious reading is the Vestal Virgins of Rome, young women devoted to the goddess Vesta, who Pastoureau says dressed entirely in white [2][3]. That would make the name a hint of purity rather than a purple, which fits a muted shade this far from true white [1][2].

On screen the swatch is a grey-pink mauve, within about six units of [[mauve]] and [[mountbatten-pink]] [1]. The one other place our books use the word is a Roman story in which a Vestal is the mother of Romulus and Remus, with no mention of color [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive, a color within six units of this one covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 14 of 23,781 paintings, led by Sartorio's 1915 self-portrait at about a quarter of the picture [5]. The earliest match is a 1600 Madonna and Child [5]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test [5].
